name: Jainism
era: From at least the 6th century BCE to today
line: Harm nothing that lives, own little and allow that others may also be right.

quote.text: I forgive all living beings. May all living beings forgive me. I have friendship with all and enmity with none.
quote.source: Khamemi savve jive, from the Pratikramana Sutra; a common English rendering

quotes.text: All breathing, existing, living, sentient creatures should not be slain, nor treated with violence, nor abused, nor tormented, nor driven away.
quotes.source: Acaranga Sutra 1.4.1, trans. Hermann Jacobi, Sacred Books of the East, 1884

quotes.text: Souls render service to one another.
quotes.source: Parasparopagraho jivanam, Tattvartha Sutra 5.21; the motto of the Jain emblem

quotes.text: Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct together are the path to liberation.
quotes.source: Tattvartha Sutra 1.1, in its common English rendering

quotes.text: The essence of the conduct of a wise person is that they do not injure anything.
quotes.source: Sutrakritanga 1.1.4.10, after the translation of Hermann Jacobi, 1895

words.usage: The first vow and the centre of the religion. It covers thought and speech as well as action, and every form of life.
One who has overcome anger, pride, deceit and greed. Jains are the followers of the Jinas.
One of the twenty-four teachers of this age who show the crossing over the river of rebirth.
Every living thing has one, from a person to a drop of water, and all are equal in their nature.
Matter, space, time and the principles of motion and rest. Karma belongs here.

words.meaning: Subtle matter that clings to the soul
words.usage: For Jains it is a physical substance. Passion makes the soul sticky, and action brings the dust.
The soul, freed of all karma, rises to the top of the universe and stays in perfect knowledge and bliss.
Reality has countless aspects, and no single statement captures it. A reason for humility in argument.
Every claim should be qualified: in some respect it is so, in some respect it is not.
Limiting what one owns and loosening attachment to it. The fifth vow.
The second vow. Truth that would cause harm is to be left unsaid.
The third vow: take nothing that is not freely given.
The fourth vow. Celibacy for monks and nuns, faithfulness for householders.
The five vows as kept by lay people, within the limits of family and working life.
The same five vows kept absolutely by monks and nuns.
A daily period of forty-eight minutes spent in stillness, treating all beings alike.
The rite of reviewing and repenting harm done, performed daily by the devout and yearly by almost everyone.

words.meaning: May my wrongs be without effect
words.usage: Said to everyone one knows on the last day of Paryushana, asking pardon for any hurt caused.
The most important Jain prayer. It bows to five kinds of worthy beings and names no person and asks for nothing.
Wandering ascetics who own almost nothing, travel on foot and eat what they are given.
A lay woman is a shravika. The four-part community is monks, nuns, laymen and laywomen.
The branch whose monks go naked, having given up even clothing.
The branch whose monks and nuns wear plain white cloth.
Going without food for a day or more. Fasting burns off old karma and is practised by lay people of all ages.
A vow taken at the very end of life, with permission, to stop eating and meet death in calm. Rare and strictly regulated.
The Shvetambara word. Digambaras say mandir or basadi.
The complete knowledge a soul has when all obscuring karma is gone.
Above all the gift of food to ascetics and of safety to living beings, called abhaya dana.
The spirit behind Jain animal hospitals and bird shelters.
The usual Jain greeting.

practices.name: Morning salutation
practices.instructions: On waking, sit up with your palms together. Bow in your mind to five kinds of people: those who have conquered themselves, those who are fully free, the leaders of communities of practice, the teachers, and all those anywhere who live with discipline. Take a breath for each. Then rise. The salutation asks nothing for yourself.
practices.why: The Namokar Mantra is the central prayer of Jainism, honouring qualities rather than a creator. Reciting it on waking is a daily habit in Jain homes.
variations: Say it aloud, slowly, nine times.
Say it silently while looking at the sky.
Learn the first line in Prakrit.

practices.name: Careful walking
practices.instructions: For ten minutes walk as a Jain ascetic does. Look at the ground a few steps ahead. Do not tread on anything alive if you can see it: ants, snails, worms after rain, seedlings in a crack. Slow down enough to make this possible. If you find something in your path, step around it or move it gently aside. Say to yourself: I will harm nothing that lives.
practices.why: Jain monks and nuns sweep the path before them to avoid stepping on small beings. Walking with this care is the most direct way to feel ahimsa in the body.
variations: Walk a short loop at your slowest.
Do it barefoot on a clean floor.
Lift a snail from a path to the grass.

practices.name: Set a limit
practices.instructions: Each morning set one limit for the day and keep it. I will eat only five different things. I will spend nothing. I will not travel beyond my neighbourhood. I will use my phone for one hour. I will speak only when it is useful. Write it down. At night, note whether you kept it. Keep the limit gentle and safe for your health.
practices.why: Jain lay people take small daily vows to limit consumption and travel. Self-chosen limits teach how little is needed.
variations: Limit the clothes you wear to what you have on.
Limit your screen to one hour.
Limit the number of words you use in messages.

practices.name: Water with care
practices.instructions: Pour your drinking water for the day through a clean cloth into a jug or bottle, to catch anything small, and return what the cloth catches to the source, a plant or a stream. Jains traditionally boil or filter water for the same reason. Drink the first glass slowly and notice that every glass holds living things.
practices.why: Straining water is an old Jain custom to avoid harming tiny beings. Even a symbolic version makes you aware of what you drink and what lives in it.
variations: Filter the water with a tea strainer.
Water a plant with what is left in glasses.
Drink a whole glass of water first thing.

practices.name: Free the little ones
practices.instructions: If you find an insect, a spider or a beetle in the house today, do not kill it. Catch it under a cup with a card slid beneath and carry it outdoors. Say: go well. If none turn up, check a window ledge or sweep a corner gently and see who lives with you. Jiv daya, compassion for living beings, begins at home.
practices.why: Jiv daya, compassion for all living beings, is the practical side of ahimsa. Jains rescue insects as a matter of course, and it makes the house a kinder place.
variations: Rescue a spider and watch it go.
Move a worm from a pavement after rain.
Leave a window open for a bee.

practices.name: A harmless first word
practices.instructions: Make the first words you speak today true, kind and necessary. Wait until you have something to say that passes all three tests. Greet people with a smile before a word if you need to. Satya, truth, and ahimsa, non-harm, in speech: the rule of this Onda is to say only what is true and harmless.
practices.why: Jain ethics apply to speech as well as action. Starting the day with a considered word sets the tone for the rest of it.
variations: Hold your tongue for the first ten minutes at home.
Begin with a thank you.
Pause before every reply for an hour.

practices.name: Samayika: forty-eight still minutes
practices.instructions: Sit on the floor or a chair in a quiet place and resolve not to move from it, nor to do, buy, send or plan anything, for a set time. The traditional period is forty-eight minutes. Start with twenty. Let the mind rest on equanimity: the same towards friend and stranger, praise and blame. Do not be alarmed by itches or thoughts; let them pass. Sit comfortably and stop if you feel unwell.
practices.why: Samayika is the Jain practice of equanimity, done daily by many lay people. Staying still for a set time teaches how much of life is the urge to move.
variations: Sit for ten minutes only, but every day.
Sit in a place with a view of the sky.
Sit with a plain cloth under you.

practices.name: Let go of one thing
practices.instructions: Choose one thing you own and do not need: a book unread for years, a shirt, a gadget, a kitchen item. Give it to someone who will use it, or take it to a donation point today. Notice any reluctance. Aparigraha, non-possessiveness, is one of the great vows. The rule of this Onda is to own less tonight than this morning.
practices.why: Aparigraha, not clinging to possessions, is a central Jain virtue. Giving away one thing at a time is a gentle, steady way to practise it.
variations: Give away something you like.
Clear one shelf completely.
Hand it over in person.

practices.name: Argue the other side
practices.instructions: Pick an opinion you hold firmly. Write down the best argument for the opposite, as a person who held it would put it. Then find one part of it that is true. Anekantavada, the doctrine of many-sidedness, holds that reality is too rich for a single view. Grant that the other view may be partly right. Say it aloud to someone if you can.
practices.why: Anekantavada, the many-sided view, is Jainism’s special contribution to the world’s thought. It encourages humility and respectful disagreement.
variations: Do it for a disagreement with a family member.
Do it with a newspaper opinion you dislike.
Ask someone to argue your side back to you.

practices.name: Water for the creatures
practices.instructions: Put out a shallow dish of fresh water and a handful of grain or seeds for the birds, bees and small animals near you. Place it in the shade and wash it daily. Jains have long supported shelters for animals and bird feeders in towns. Stay quiet and watch from a distance for a while. Do no harm.
practices.why: Jiv daya, compassion for living things, is put into practice in Jain communities through bird feeders and animal shelters. A saucer of water is the smallest version.
variations: Visit an animal shelter or give a donation.
Put out water for bees.
Count the visitors you get.

practices.name: A simple, light meal
practices.instructions: Eat one meal today that is simple, vegetarian and plain: dal, rice, a vegetable, a flatbread. Take only what you will eat and finish it all. Chew slowly and stop when you are not quite full. Wash up with as little water as you can. The Jain table is a place for taking only what is needed.
practices.why: Jain food is vegetarian and carefully chosen to avoid harm. A simple meal eaten with attention embodies the whole ethic.
variations: Leave out onions and garlic for the day.
Skip a dessert you do not need.
Cook enough to feed only the people at the table.

practices.name: One hour of true words
practices.instructions: For the next hour say only what is true and harmless. If you cannot say it truthfully and kindly, stay silent. Notice how many small exaggerations, flattering lies and sharp remarks you would normally make. If you slip, note it, say sorry and go on. Satya, truthfulness, is a vow; this is a small trial of it.
practices.why: Truthfulness is one of the five vows of Jainism. Even a short period of watching speech shows how automatic our small untruths are.
variations: Do it at work.
Do it with family.
Note your slips in a notebook.

practices.name: The evening turning back
practices.instructions: Before sunset if you can, finish eating. Later, sit and go back through the day from the morning. Recall each harm you did, in act, word or thought: the insect, the sharp reply, the wasteful purchase, the contempt you did not voice. Do not defend yourself. Say aloud, micchami dukkadam: may any harm I did be undone. Then resolve one small thing for tomorrow.
practices.why: Pratikramana, literally turning back, is the Jain daily review and confession, often done at dusk. It is honest, brief and without drama.
variations: Write the harms and the good in two columns.
Do it standing by an open window.
Do it with a family member who is also reviewing.

practices.name: An early supper
practices.instructions: Finish your evening meal before sunset or at least three hours before bed. Eat lightly and at a regular time. Chauvihar, the vow of not eating after dark, is kept by many Jains to avoid harming insects drawn to lamps. Try a gentle version: set a time and stop eating at it, without strain. If you have a health condition that needs food at set times, follow your doctor’s advice instead.
practices.why: Eating before sunset is a Jain custom that fits well with digestion and rest. It also leaves the evening free.
variations: Eat supper in daylight on the porch.
Have a warm drink instead of a late snack.
Make the early meal an occasion.

practices.name: Micchami dukkadam
practices.instructions: Ask forgiveness from someone you may have wronged, with simple words: if I hurt you in any way, I am sorry. Say it in person, by phone or in a message. Forgive anyone who has asked, or anyone you still hold something against, at least silently. The Jain rule is to ask forgiveness before you sleep, and to bear no grudge.
practices.why: Micchami dukkadam, may my wrong be in vain, is said by Jains during Paryushana and in daily review. Asking and giving forgiveness is a daily skill.
variations: Send three short messages.
Say it to a family member.
Forgive someone and tell no one.

practices.name: Own less tonight
practices.instructions: Before you go to bed, take one item out of your house. A broken thing, an old magazine, a drawer of cables, a set of clothes you do not wear. Take it out now: to the bin, to a charity bag by the door, to a neighbour. The rule of this Onda is to own less tonight than this morning.
practices.why: Aparigraha is practised by letting go of small things regularly. A daily item adds up to a lighter life.
variations: Clear one drawer.
Photograph a keepsake and let the object go.
Choose something someone will use.

practices.name: Listen to the Bhaktamar Stotra
practices.instructions: Play the Bhaktamar Stotra, a Sanskrit hymn of praise composed about thirteen hundred years ago, in a recording by a Jain chorus. Sit upright and listen for ten minutes. Follow a translation if you can. The hymn is said to have been composed by Acharya Manatunga and is recited by Jains each morning and evening.
practices.why: The Bhaktamar Stotra is one of the best-loved Jain hymns, praising the first tirthankara. Its steady rhythm makes it good for listening.
variations: Read the English translation while listening.
Listen with the lights off.
Hum along with the last verse.

practices.name: The elephant and the blind men
practices.instructions: Tell the story of the elephant and the blind men to someone, or read it aloud. Each touches a different part and insists the elephant is a rope, a pillar, a fan, a wall. Tell it with voices. Then ask: where in your life are you holding a part and calling it the whole? This is the many-sided view, told as a tale.
practices.why: The tale of the blind men and the elephant is told in Jain and Buddhist traditions. Anekantavada uses it to teach that every view captures only part of the truth.
variations: Tell it to a child.
Add a fifth man who sees the whole.
Use it in a real disagreement.

practices.name: A Jain-style feast without roots
practices.instructions: Cook a meal in the Jain style for friends, avoiding root vegetables such as onion, garlic, potato and carrot, since pulling them up kills the plant. Use lentils, rice, gourds, beans, leafy vegetables and fruit, with ginger-free spices if you prefer. Eat it in daylight. A Jain meal is a creative challenge that shows how much flavour is possible.
practices.why: Jain cooking avoids root vegetables, honey and anything that harms living beings, yet is rich and varied. Cooking it is a pleasing puzzle.
variations: Make a raw banana curry.
Serve khakhra with chutney.
Share the recipe with a guest.

practices.name: A day of forgiveness letters
practices.instructions: On a free day, write short letters of forgiveness to five people: ask pardon from those you may have hurt and offer it to those who hurt you. Be specific and brief. Send some and keep others to yourself if you prefer. In Jain communities the day of Samvatsari is for exactly this. Finish with a deep breath and a feeling of lightness.
practices.why: The last day of Paryushana is a day of asking and giving forgiveness, with a greeting of micchami dukkadam to everyone. A private version brings the same relief.
variations: Write one letter to your younger self.
Write to someone you have not spoken with for years.
Phone someone instead of writing.

immersePlan.name: Read Jainism: An Introduction
immersePlan.text: Read a chapter of Jeffery Long’s clear introduction to the history and ideas of Jainism. Note one idea that is new to you.

immersePlan.name: Read from the Acaranga Sutra
immersePlan.text: Read a passage of the oldest Jain scripture, about how to move through the world without harm. Notice how detailed the care is.

immersePlan.name: Read the Tattvartha Sutra
immersePlan.text: Read a few of Umasvati’s short aphorisms on the nature of the soul and the world. Pick one to think about for the day.

immersePlan.name: Watch Ship of Theseus
immersePlan.text: Watch Anand Gandhi’s 2012 film about identity, in which a blind photographer, a monk and a stockbroker meet through an organ transplant. The monk is a Jain on a hunger strike over animal testing, so notice how the film treats his convictions.

immersePlan.name: Watch Ahimsa: Non-Violence
immersePlan.text: Watch Michael Tobias’s documentary on Jain life and the ethic of non-harm. Note the images of everyday care.

immersePlan.name: Watch The Story of India, episode two
immersePlan.text: Watch the BBC episode in which Michael Wood visits the cave where Mahavira and the Buddha taught, and the thinkers of sixth-century BCE India.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Namokar Mantra
immersePlan.text: Play a recording of the central Jain prayer, sung by a choir or a single voice. Sit still for its five lines.

immersePlan.name: Listen to the Bhaktamar Stotra
immersePlan.text: Play the Sanskrit hymn in praise of the first tirthankara. Follow the translation or the rhythm.

immersePlan.name: Listen to Jain stavans
immersePlan.text: Play devotional songs in Gujarati sung by Jain singers. Notice the simple, steady melodies.

immersePlan.name: Look at Gommateshwara
immersePlan.text: Look at pictures of the 17-metre naked statue of Bahubali at Shravanabelagola, carved from a single granite rock in 981. Notice the vines climbing his legs.

immersePlan.name: Look at the Dilwara Temples
immersePlan.text: Look at the marble carving of the temples at Mount Abu, so fine that it looks like lace. Choose a ceiling and look at it for five minutes.

immersePlan.name: Look at Kalpa Sutra manuscripts
immersePlan.text: Look at the brightly painted manuscripts of the lives of the tirthankaras, with gold and ultramarine. Find one with an animal in it.

immersePlan.name: Cook dal, rice and rotli
immersePlan.text: Cook a simple plate of lentils, rice and flatbread, with a vegetable. Eat it in daylight and finish all of it.

immersePlan.name: Cook khichdi and kadhi
immersePlan.text: Cook rice and lentils together, and a spiced yogurt curry on the side. It is the comfort meal of Gujarat.

immersePlan.name: Taste khakhra
immersePlan.text: Crunch on thin roasted wheat crispbread, a travelling food of Jain families. Eat it with chutney or a cup of tea.

immersePlan.name: Drink boiled water
immersePlan.text: Boil water, let it cool and drink it through the day. Jains do this to avoid harming tiny life in raw water. Drink a glass slowly and think about what it took to make.

immersePlan.name: Drink chaas
immersePlan.text: Whisk yogurt with cold water, salt and roasted cumin until frothy. It is the cooling drink of Gujarat and Rajasthan. Share a glass.

immersePlan.name: Drink warm milk with saffron
immersePlan.text: Warm milk with a few threads of saffron and a pinch of cardamom, and drink it before bed. It is a quiet, golden drink.

immersePlan.name: Eat before sunset
immersePlan.text: Have your evening meal in daylight today, as many Jains do. Sit and notice how the evening changes when supper is early.

immersePlan.name: Learn about giving food to monks
immersePlan.text: Read about how Jain households offer pure food to monks and nuns on their rounds. Then give a plate of food to someone who needs it.

immersePlan.name: Ask someone’s pardon
immersePlan.text: Say micchami dukkadam, may any wrong be undone, to one person, in person or by message. Ask and listen.

immersePlan.name: Play Gyan Chaupar
immersePlan.text: Play the Jain game of knowledge, a cousin of snakes and ladders in which virtues lift you and vices drop you. Draw the board and play with a friend.

immersePlan.name: Play chaupar
immersePlan.text: Play the ancient cross-shaped race game with cowries or dice, as in India for centuries. Make a board from cloth or paper.

immersePlan.name: Play Journey
immersePlan.text: Play the wordless game of a robed traveller crossing a desert to a mountain. Play it in one sitting and pay attention to your pace.

immersePlan.name: Mark Paryushana
immersePlan.text: Paryushana is an eight-to-ten-day period of reflection and forgiveness in late summer. Spend a few minutes today forgiving someone and asking forgiveness of someone.

immersePlan.name: Mark Mahavir Jayanti
immersePlan.text: Mahavir Jayanti, in March or April, marks the birth of the last tirthankara. Read a short account of his life and do one small kind act in his spirit.

immersePlan.name: Look up Shravanabelagola
immersePlan.text: Look at the hill town in Karnataka where Bahubali’s statue stands. Read about the festival held every twelve years when the statue is bathed.

immersePlan.name: Practise anekantavada
immersePlan.text: Anekantavada is the many-sided view. In one conversation today, try to state the other person’s view fairly before you give yours.

immersePlan.name: Practise aparigraha
immersePlan.text: Aparigraha is non-possessiveness. Go through one pocket, bag or drawer and remove three things you do not need.

immersePlan.name: Say micchami dukkadam
immersePlan.text: Say micchami dukkadam to someone, meaning may any wrong I did be in vain. Say it kindly and mean it.

rules.why: No meat, fish or eggs, no killing of insects, no cruelty in word. When in doubt, choose the course that hurts less.

rules.text: Say only what is true and harmless
rules.why: No lies, no exaggeration, no truth told in order to wound. Otherwise keep silent.
Nothing borrowed without asking, no extra from the office, no unearned credit.

rules.text: Own less tonight than this morning
rules.why: Give, return or release one thing each day. Set a ceiling on what you will acquire.

rules.text: Grant that the other view may be partly right
rules.why: In every disagreement today, state the other side fairly before your own.
Review the day, own the harm and let no quarrel last past sunset.

read.title: That Which Is (Tattvartha Sutra)
read.creator: Umasvati, trans. Nathmal Tatia
read.why: The one text all Jain branches accept: the whole system in 350 terse aphorisms, with the commentaries of each tradition.

read.title: Jaina Sutras, part 1: the Acaranga Sutra
read.creator: trans. Hermann Jacobi
read.why: The oldest Jain scripture. It opens by asking the reader to recognise that earth, water, fire, air and plants are alive.

read.title: The Jains
read.creator: Paul Dundas
read.why: The standard scholarly account of history, doctrine and practice.

read.title: Jainism: An Introduction
read.creator: Jeffery D. Long
read.why: A clear short book with good chapters on many-sidedness.

read.title: The Jaina Path of Purification
read.creator: Padmanabh S. Jaini
read.why: How the path works, stage by stage, by a scholar raised in the tradition.

read.title: Life Force: The World of Jainism
read.creator: Michael Tobias
read.why: A naturalist’s warm account of Jain ethics toward animals and the earth.

watch.title: Ship of Theseus
watch.creator: Anand Gandhi
watch.why: Three stories set in Mumbai. In the second a monk who is suing to stop animal testing falls ill and must decide whether to take medicine. Closely modelled on Jain thought.

watch.title: Ahimsa: Non-Violence
watch.creator: Michael Tobias
watch.why: A documentary made for American public television and still the best film introduction to Jain life.

watch.title: The Story of India, episode 2: The Power of Ideas
watch.creator: Michael Wood, BBC
watch.why: Sets Mahavira and the Buddha in the world of the Ganges plain in the fifth century BCE.

watch.title: Mahamastakabhisheka films
watch.creator: News and documentary footage
watch.why: Every twelve years the great statue at Shravanabelagola is bathed in milk, saffron and sandalwood from a scaffold. Watch any good record of it.

listen.title: Namokar Mantra
listen.creator: Many recordings; try Lata Mangeshkar’s
listen.why: The salutation prayer sung slowly. Nine lines in Prakrit.

listen.title: Bhaktamar Stotra
listen.creator: Acharya Manatunga; many recordings
listen.why: Forty-eight Sanskrit verses in praise of the first Tirthankara. Legend says each verse broke one of the chains that held the poet.

listen.title: Stavans
listen.creator: Jain devotional singers
listen.why: Hymns in Gujarati and Hindi sung in temples and at home, often to familiar folk tunes.

listen.title: Uvasaggaharam Stotra
listen.creator: Attributed to Bhadrabahu
listen.why: A short Prakrit hymn to Parshvanatha, recited for protection.

art.title: Gommateshwara (Bahubali)
art.creator: Shravanabelagola, Karnataka
art.why: A figure seventeen metres tall cut from one block of granite on a hilltop. He stands in meditation so long that creepers have grown up his limbs.

art.title: The Dilwara Temples
art.creator: Mount Abu, Rajasthan
art.why: Plain outside. Inside, white marble carved so thin that the ceilings look like lace.

art.title: The Adinatha Temple
art.creator: Ranakpur, Rajasthan
art.why: A marble hall on 1,444 pillars, no two carved alike.

art.title: Illustrated Kalpa Sutra manuscripts
art.creator: Western India
art.why: Lives of the Tirthankaras painted in red, gold and blue, with the characteristic eye that projects beyond the face. In many museum collections.

eat.title: Dal, rice and rotli
eat.creator: Lentils, rice, flatbread and a green vegetable
eat.why: The everyday Gujarati Jain plate. No onion, garlic, potato or carrot, because pulling a root kills the plant and the small lives around it.

eat.title: Khichdi and kadhi
eat.creator: Rice and lentils with a spiced yogurt soup
eat.why: A plain supper, eaten before dark.

eat.title: Khakhra
eat.creator: Thin roasted wheat crispbread
eat.why: Dry food that keeps for weeks and suits fasting days and travel.

eat.title: Raw banana curry
eat.creator: Green plantain cooked with spices
eat.why: The Jain stand-in for potato in many dishes.

drink.title: Boiled water
drink.creator: Boiled, cooled and drunk within the day
drink.why: Monks, nuns and strict lay people drink only water that has been boiled, to avoid harming the minute lives in it.

drink.title: Warm milk with saffron
drink.creator: Kesar dudh
drink.why: Given to break a long fast gently.

customs.title: Eating before sunset
customs.creator: Chauvihar
customs.why: Cooking and eating stop at dusk, when insects are drawn to lamps and food and cannot be seen.

customs.title: The mouth cloth
customs.creator: Muhpatti
customs.why: A small white cloth held or tied before the mouth during prayer, and worn always by some ascetics, to avoid harming life in the air.

customs.title: Giving food to ascetics
customs.creator: Gochari
customs.why: Monks and nuns collect a little from many homes, as a cow grazes, so that no household is burdened. To give is an honour.

customs.title: Asking pardon
customs.creator: Kshamapana
customs.why: At the end of Paryushana Jains contact family, friends, colleagues and rivals to ask forgiveness for the year.

games.title: Gyan Chaupar
games.creator: Board game · India
games.why: The game of knowledge, ancestor of snakes and ladders. The oldest surviving boards are Jain, with eighty-four squares mapping the soul’s climb from the hells to liberation.

games.title: Chaupar
games.creator: Board game · India
games.why: A cross-shaped race game played with long dice. Jain texts caution against gambling, so play for nothing.

games.title: Journey
games.creator: Video game · thatgamecompany
games.why: A robed figure crosses a desert toward a mountain. There is no combat and no speech, and strangers can only help each other. Not Jain, but close in spirit.

festivals.title: Paryushana
festivals.creator: August or September, eight or ten days
festivals.why: The main festival: fasting, scripture and repentance, ending in the day of universal forgiveness. Digambaras call their ten days Das Lakshana.

festivals.title: Mahavir Jayanti
festivals.creator: March or April
festivals.why: The birth of Mahavira, marked with processions, giving and the freeing of animals.

festivals.title: Diwali
festivals.creator: October or November
festivals.why: For Jains the night lamps were lit to mark Mahavira’s final liberation. The new year begins the next day.

festivals.title: Mahamastakabhisheka
festivals.creator: Every 12 years; last in 2018
festivals.why: The head-anointing of the Bahubali statue at Shravanabelagola. The next is expected in 2030.

places.title: Shravanabelagola
places.creator: Karnataka, India
places.why: Climb about six hundred rock-cut steps barefoot to the great statue. By tradition the emperor Chandragupta Maurya ended his life as a monk on the hill opposite.

places.title: Palitana
places.creator: Gujarat, India
places.why: Shatrunjaya hill, with some nine hundred marble temples on its summit and 3,800 steps up. No one may stay on the hill overnight, and the town below is meat-free by law.

places.title: Ranakpur
places.creator: Rajasthan, India
places.why: The temple of a thousand pillars in a quiet wooded valley. Open to visitors from midday.

places.title: Dilwara, Mount Abu
places.creator: Rajasthan, India
places.why: Five marble temples in a hill station. Photography is not allowed inside.

places.title: Jain Center of Greater Phoenix, Oshwal Centre and others
places.creator: Diaspora temples in the US, UK and Kenya
places.why: Jain communities abroad have built fine temples and usually welcome visitors. Ask about dress, and leave leather outside.

ethics.title: Non-violence
ethics.text: All living beings want to live and none wants to suffer. From this follows a strict vegetarian diet, care in every movement and professions chosen to do least harm.
ethics.practice: Trace one thing you used today back to any harm in its making. Find a gentler alternative.

ethics.title: Truth
ethics.text: Speak what is true, pleasant and beneficial. A truth that would lead to violence is better withheld.
ethics.practice: Go the whole day without a single exaggeration.

ethics.title: Not taking
ethics.text: Whatever has not been freely given is not yours, including time, attention and ideas.
ethics.practice: Give credit today to someone whose work you used.

ethics.title: Restraint of desire
ethics.text: Sexual and sensual restraint keep the mind clear and others unharmed. For householders this means faithfulness and moderation.
ethics.practice: Notice one craving today and wait it out.

ethics.title: Non-possession
ethics.text: Possessions tie the soul down, and what we hoard is taken from others. Lay Jains set a ceiling on their wealth and give away the surplus.
ethics.practice: Decide what enough is for one category of things you own. Give away what is over.

ethics.title: Forgiveness
ethics.text: Anger binds karma faster than anything. Forgiving and asking forgiveness are counted as marks of strength.
ethics.practice: Send the message you have been putting off: I am sorry, or I forgive you.

philosophy.title: Everything is alive
philosophy.text: Jain thought finds souls in people and animals and also in plants, water, fire, air and earth, ranked by how many senses they have. No act is free of harm, so the aim is always to do less.
philosophy.practice: Count the kinds of living things your lunch involved.

philosophy.title: Karma as matter
philosophy.text: Karma here is a fine substance that sticks to the soul when it acts from passion, as dust sticks to an oiled cloth. Stop the passion and the dust stops. Practise restraint and the old dust wears off.
philosophy.practice: Catch one moment of anger, pride, deceit or greed today and name it as it happens.

philosophy.title: Many-sidedness
philosophy.text: A thing has endless aspects, and each viewpoint grasps some of them. The parable is of blind men and an elephant: each is right about his part and wrong to claim the whole.
philosophy.practice: Take a position you oppose and write three things that are true in it.

philosophy.title: In some respect
philosophy.text: Jain logicians taught that a careful statement begins with maybe, or in some respect. A pot exists as clay and here, and does not exist as gold or there.
philosophy.practice: Add in some respect to your strongest opinion today and see what changes.

philosophy.title: Self-reliance
philosophy.text: There is no creator and no saviour who can lift the weight. The Tirthankaras show the ford and each soul crosses by its own effort. The same fact makes every soul capable of freedom.
philosophy.practice: Do one hard thing today that you have been waiting for someone else to fix.

philosophy.title: The three jewels
philosophy.text: Right faith, right knowledge and right conduct. Seeing truly, understanding accurately and acting on it. They are three legs of one stool, and none stands alone.
philosophy.practice: Find a belief of yours that your conduct contradicts.

philosophy.title: The soul is equal in all
philosophy.text: Every soul, from a mite to a master, has the same nature: knowledge, perception, energy and bliss, more or less covered over. Difference lies in the covering only.
philosophy.practice: Look at one creature you dislike and consider that it wants to live.

philosophy.title: Stopping and shedding
philosophy.text: The path has two movements. Samvara stops new karma coming in, by vows and carefulness. Nirjara burns off the old, by fasting, study and meditation.
philosophy.practice: Choose one inflow to stop today: a habit of speech, a feed, a purchase.

intro: Jainism is one of the oldest religions in the world still practised, and one of the smallest: about five million people, most of them in India. Its influence is far larger than its numbers. It has carried the idea of non-violence further than any other tradition, and through Gandhi, who grew up among Jains in Gujarat, that idea changed the twentieth century.

Jains follow the Jinas, the conquerors: human beings who overcame their own anger, pride, deceit and greed and so became free. There are twenty-four in each great cycle of time. They are also called Tirthankaras, makers of the ford across the river of rebirth. The most recent, Mahavira, was born a prince in what is now Bihar, left home at thirty, spent twelve years in severe self-discipline and taught for thirty more. He was an older contemporary of the Buddha.

The teaching begins from a simple observation: every living thing wants to live and does not want to suffer. Jains find life everywhere, in animals and plants and also in water, fire, air and earth. Each life is a soul, equal in nature to every other. Souls are weighed down by karma, which Jains understand as a fine matter that sticks to the soul when it acts with passion. The way to freedom is to stop the inflow and wear away what has gathered, through right faith, right knowledge and right conduct.

Conduct means five vows: not to harm, not to lie, not to steal, to be chaste and to renounce possessions. Monks and nuns keep them completely. They own nothing, walk barefoot from village to village, eat once a day what they are given and sweep the ground before they sit. Lay people keep them as far as family and working life allow. All Jains are vegetarian. Many do not eat after dark or eat root vegetables, and many fast regularly.

A second great idea is many-sidedness. Reality is complex, and every viewpoint catches only part of it. So Jain philosophers trained themselves to state an opponent’s case fairly and to qualify their own. It is non-violence applied to thinking.

This Onda borrows the lay Jain’s day in a mild form: a morning salutation, ten minutes of careful walking, a period of stillness, one freely chosen limit and an evening review that ends in asking forgiveness. You will eat no meat for its length. You are a guest. The long fasts and the ascetic life belong to people formed by the tradition and guided by its teachers, and they are not to be imitated.
guide.origin: The Ganges plain of north India; today mainly Gujarat, Rajasthan, Maharashtra and Karnataka
guide.era: Mahavira taught in the 6th or 5th century BCE; Jains hold the teaching to be eternal

figures.name: Rishabhanatha
figures.bio: The first Tirthankara of this age, also called Adinatha. Tradition credits him with teaching farming, crafts and writing before he renounced the world.

figures.name: Parshvanatha
figures.bio: The twenty-third Tirthankara, shown under a canopy of cobra hoods. Probably a historical teacher whose followers Mahavira’s parents belonged to.

figures.name: Mahavira
figures.dates: traditionally 599 to 527 BCE; many scholars place him about a century later
figures.bio: Born Vardhamana. He left his family, endured twelve years of hardship without retaliating against anyone and reorganised the community that still exists.

figures.name: Indrabhuti Gautama
figures.bio: A learned brahmin who came to debate Mahavira and stayed as his chief disciple. He is remembered each Diwali.

figures.name: Bhadrabahu
figures.bio: The last teacher said to have known all the scriptures. Tradition says he led monks south during a famine, taking with him the retired emperor Chandragupta Maurya.

figures.name: Kundakunda
figures.bio: The most revered Digambara thinker, who taught the difference between the soul as it truly is and as it appears.

figures.name: Umasvati
figures.bio: Author of the Tattvartha Sutra, the first Jain work in Sanskrit and the only one accepted by every branch.

figures.name: Haribhadra
figures.bio: A prolific scholar-monk who wrote with unusual fairness about other schools and said he sided with whoever’s teaching was sound.

figures.name: Hemachandra
figures.bio: Monk, grammarian, poet and adviser to the kings of Gujarat. Under his influence the state banned animal slaughter.

figures.name: Shrimad Rajchandra
figures.bio: A jeweller, poet and mystic of Gujarat. Gandhi called him his guide and wrote to him with his doubts from South Africa.

history.detail: An ascetic teacher at Varanasi founds an order with four vows. Mahavira is born into a family that follows him.
He renounces at thirty, reaches omniscience at forty-two and teaches in Magadha until his death at Pavapuri at seventy-two. He adds chastity as a fifth vow.
According to Digambara tradition, Bhadrabahu leads part of the community to Karnataka to escape a twelve-year famine. Differences between those who left and those who stayed begin to harden.
A Jain king records his deeds in an inscription in the Udayagiri caves in Odisha, one of the earliest datable pieces of Jain history.
The community separates into Digambaras, whose monks go naked and who hold the original scriptures lost, and Shvetambaras, who wear white and preserve a canon.
Shvetambara monks meet in Gujarat and commit their scriptures to writing in the form still used.
The minister Chamundaraya has a seventeen-metre figure of Bahubali carved from the hilltop. It becomes the great pilgrimage site of the south.

history.what: Marble and learning in the west
history.detail: Jain merchants and ministers in Gujarat and Rajasthan build the Dilwara temples. Hemachandra flourishes at the Solanki court.
Lonka Shah, a scribe in Ahmedabad, criticises image worship. The Sthanakvasi and later the Terapanthi orders, who use no temples, descend from his protest.
The monk Hiravijaya impresses the emperor Akbar, who bans animal slaughter during the Paryushana festival.
Virchand Gandhi, a young lawyer, represents Jainism at the Parliament of the World’s Religions and lectures across America.
Jains settle in East Africa, Britain and North America. Mohandas Gandhi applies non-violence to politics. In 1974 the branches agree on a shared emblem and a common text, Saman Suttam.

concepts.text: Non-violence in thought, word and deed.
concepts.detail: Jain texts analyse harm in detail: done oneself, caused through others or approved; by body, speech or mind. Intention matters most, and care is always required.
The universe consists of souls and five kinds of non-soul. It was never created and will never end. Souls are classed by the number of senses they have, from one to five.
There are eight main kinds, which obscure knowledge, produce pleasure and pain, fix lifespan and so on. Passions are the glue. Even a good deed binds if done with attachment.
Together they make up the path. Faith here means a clear view of how things are and trust in those who have seen it.
Non-violence, truth, not stealing, chastity and non-possession. Kept in a limited form by lay people, with seven supporting vows, and absolutely by ascetics.
Things are both permanent in substance and changing in form. One-sided views are partial truths taken for the whole. The doctrine underlies Jain tolerance.
Of anything one can say: in a way it is, in a way it is not, in a way both, in a way it cannot be said, and three combinations of these.
They have left the world entirely and cannot answer prayers. Their images are honoured as reminders of what a soul can become.
The gunasthanas map progress from wrong belief through the vows to omniscience and final release. Gyan Chaupar boards are pictures of it.

facts.text: The raised open hand of the Jain emblem carries a wheel with the word ahimsa in its centre. It means stop and consider before you act.
Jains run animal hospitals called panjrapoles, some of which have been open for centuries. The one beside the Red Fort in Delhi treats birds free of charge.
Jains are about four in every thousand Indians and have long had the highest literacy rate of any religious community in the country.
Some Jain libraries, such as those of Jaisalmer and Patan, preserved palm-leaf manuscripts for a thousand years, including many non-Jain works that survive nowhere else.
The swastika is a central Jain symbol. Its four arms stand for the four states of rebirth: heavenly, human, animal and hellish.
Farming is traditionally avoided because ploughing kills creatures in the soil, which is one reason Jains became traders, bankers and jewellers.

sensitivity.note: Jainism is a living religion with a demanding ascetic core. This Onda offers a mild version of a lay person’s discipline. It does not ask for long fasts or for anything that could harm your health, and it is no substitute for the guidance of the Jain community.
requiredCaveats: Digambara, Shvetambara, Sthanakvasi and Terapanthi Jains differ on images, scriptures and practice.
Fasting and not eating after dark are optional here. Do not attempt them if you are unwell, pregnant or have a history of disordered eating.
The fast to death is a rare, regulated religious act at the natural end of life. It is neither suicide nor a practice for outsiders to romanticise.
Images of the Tirthankaras are sacred. In temples, remove shoes and leather and follow local guidance.
